stories.title: Hilton-Branded Hotel Offerings to Anchor Former Nashville Office Tower
stories.excerpt: Office space in the downtown Fifth Third Center is slated to be converted into hundreds of hotel and timeshare units. The Nashville Business Journal reports that the rooms will be part of Hilton’s LXR Hotels & Resorts brand and Hilton Grand Vacations. Pivot Real Estate Partners and Hastings Architecture are helming the conversion of the 30-story tower. The tower, located at 424 Church St., is slated to offer a total of 483 rooms, including 318 hotel rooms and 165 timeshare units. Other features of the future hotel and timeshare tower include separate amenity spaces for hotel guests and timeshare owners, as well as a ballroom. A lobby bar, all-day restaurant and retail and coffee space are planned for the building’s ground level. The building’s plaza is planned to feature an outdoor bar with a food-and-beverage concept. Pivot Real Estate Partners bought Fifth Third Center for $55.25 million last August. The post Hilton-Branded Hotel Offerings to Anchor Former Nashville Office Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Pivot Real Estate Partners converting 30-story Nashville office tower to 483 hotel/timeshare units
Fifth Third Center at 424 Church St. acquired August 2024 for $55.25M, now repositioned
LXR Hotels & Resorts and Hilton Grand Vacations brands anchor 318 hotel + 165 timeshare mix
stories.summary: Pivot Real Estate Partners is converting the Fifth Third Center office tower in downtown Nashville into a 483-room mixed-use hotel and timeshare property anchored by Hilton's LXR and HGV brands. The $55.25M acquisition (August 2024) is being repositioned by Pivot and Hastings Architecture to include 318 hotel rooms, 165 timeshare units, a ballroom, ground-floor food and beverage, and dual amenity spaces. The project reflects the ongoing flight from office-to-hospitality in secondary markets.
stories.impact: Office-to-hotel conversions signal persistent multifamily headwinds in Nashville's downtown: office vacancy and reduced corporate demand are redirecting capital away from housing. However, this signals strong tourism and hospitality demand in Nashville, which can indirectly support adjacent multifamily submarkets through job creation and visitor-driven demand for short-term rentals and service workers. Developers should watch whether downtown office-to-other conversions accelerate, potentially freeing up capital and labor for residential development in Nashville's fast-growing suburban markets (Williamson County, Murfreesboro).

stories.title: Arrow Adds Veteran Multifamily Lender Ari Mandelbaum to Grow Platform
stories.excerpt: Arrow Real Estate Advisors continues to ramp up its roster nearly two years after its founding. The capital markets advisory firm founded by Morris Betesh in fall 2024 has added Ari Mandelbaum, a former lender at Greystone and Dwight Capital, as a director to help grow its multifamily debt placement business, Commercial Observer has learned. “Ari brings a highly valuable perspective to Arrow given his extensive experience on the lender side of the business,” Betesh said in a statement. “His understanding of underwriting, credit and execution allows him to approach financing assignments from both sides of the table and provide clients with a deeper level of insight throughout the capital-raising process.” Mandelbaum previously held senior roles at Greystone and Dwight Capital specializing in agency and bridge loans across multifamily and other property sectors. He was at Greystone from 2011 to 2014 before a decade-long run at Dwight, where he ascended to an executive vice president role. At Arrow, Mandelbaum will focus heavily on negotiating multifamily loans while helping borrowers navigate alternative strategies. Among the multifamily deals he originated at Dwight was a $36 million bridge loan in 2023 for Latco Enterprises to refinance its Villa Annette Apartments property in Moreno Valley, Calif., CO first reported at the time. “I’m excited to join Arrow and work alongside a team with a strong track record across the commercial real estate capital markets,” Mandelbaum said in a statement. “My experience on the credit side has given me a firsthand understanding of how transactions are evaluated, structured and executed, and I look forward to applying that perspective to help Arrow’s clients navigate increasingly structured financing environments.” The addition of Mandelbaum comes on the heels of Arrow hiring Jeff Weinberg from Meridian Capital Group as a managing director, CO previously reported. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Arrow Real Estate Advisors hires Ari Mandelbaum, veteran Greystone and Dwight Capital lender
Mandelbaum led agency and bridge multifamily debt placement; EVP at Dwight for decade
Arrow founded fall 2024 by Morris Betesh; now expanding multifamily debt platform
stories.summary: Arrow Real Estate Advisors, a capital markets advisory firm founded in fall 2024, hired Ari Mandelbaum as director to expand its multifamily debt placement business. Mandelbaum spent a decade as executive vice president at Dwight Capital and earlier roles at Greystone, specializing in agency and bridge lending. Arrow founder Morris Betesh cited Mandelbaum's lender-side expertise as key to helping borrowers navigate underwriting, credit, and alternative financing strategies.
stories.impact: This hire signals strong demand for multifamily debt advisory services and suggests lender discipline is tightening post-2023 rate shock. Mandelbaum's focus on 'alternative strategies' implies that traditional agency financing windows are narrowing or becoming more selective—developers should expect more rigorous underwriting, potential recapitalization pressure, and earlier engagement with alternative lenders (life companies, CMBS, foreign capital) during the planning phase rather than at takeout.

stories.title: Florida Tech Opens $96 Million Student Dorm
stories.excerpt: Florida Tech has opened the doors of a six-story, 556-bed student housing complex on the Melbourne campus. It was funded through $96.1 million in municipal bond financing. Dubbed Crimson Crossing, it was built using a Public-Private Partnership (P3) model with Servitas Development. It took 15 months to build. The majority of the apartment-style units in the complex will be four-bedroom, two-bathroom suites equipped with full kitchens. Amenities will include a classroom area, study and lounge spaces, a multipurpose room and two outdoor courtyards designed for dining and recreation. The need for more student housing is fueled by Florida Tech’s growing student body. Traditional and online student enrollment has increased more than 27% since 2019, reaching over 10,000 students in fall 2025. During that same timeframe, first-time-in-college students have jumped over 43%, and the fall-to-fall retention rate increased from 74.3% in 2022 to 83.3% in 2025. bullets: Florida Tech opens 556-bed student housing via $96.1M municipal bond, P3 with Servitas

stories.summary: Florida Tech completed Crimson Crossing, a 556-bed, six-story student housing complex on its Melbourne campus, financed through $96.1M in municipal bonds under a public-private partnership with Servitas Development. Delivered in 15 months, the complex features primarily four-bedroom apartment-style units with full kitchens, plus amenities including classrooms, lounges, dining courtyards, and recreation spaces. FIT's enrollment growth of 27% since 2019 and first-time student jump of 43% drove the need for on-campus housing.
stories.impact: Strong institutional enrollment growth (+27% headcount, +43% first-time students) and improving retention (83.3%) indicate Florida Tech is a demographic growth engine in Brevard County. While this specific project is on-campus, it validates robust student demand in the Melbourne metro. Off-campus student housing developers should recognize FIT's trajectory as a tailwind for rental demand in surrounding areas; the university's growth trajectory suggests sustainable, recurring tenant pipeline for purpose-built or adaptive student housing in Brevard County and nearby markets.

stories.title: The Fever’s Down, But New York’s Rent-Stabilized Market Is Still Ill
stories.excerpt: New York City’s rent-stabilized housing stock has an increasingly serious economic problem. For years, the operating expenses of these buildings have been rising much faster than their revenues. Insurance premiums, real estate taxes, water and sewer charges, fuel, labor, repairs and maintenance have all increased significantly, while the ability of owners to increase rents has been severely constrained. The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 eliminated or restricted many of the mechanisms owners previously used to recover investments in their buildings, and now we have a rent freeze layered on top of that. The result is not complicated. When expenses consistently grow faster than revenue, eventually the two lines cross. Robert Knakal. PHOTO: Patrick McMullan/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images New York City’s Article XI is increasingly being discussed as one possible solution. The program can provide an extraordinary property-tax benefit to qualifying buildings for as long as 40 years, replacing conventional real estate taxes with a substantially lower PILOT, or payment in lieu of taxes. For a distressed rent-stabilized building, the impact can be dramatic. A building paying 25 percent or more of its gross revenue in real estate taxes might see that burden reduced substantially. Suddenly, a property that was barely breaking even, or even losing money, can generate positive cash flow again. For an owner facing a mortgage maturity, foreclosure or the prospect of handing the keys back to the lender, Article XI can be a lifeline. But a lifeline is not a cure. Think about a patient suffering from a serious infection and running a dangerously high fever. You give the patient Tylenol. The fever comes down. The patient feels better. Everyone is relieved. But, if you haven’t treated the infection causing the fever, what happens? Eventually, the fever comes back. Article XI can bring the financial fever down, but it does not necessarily cure the und
bullets: NYC rent-stabilized buildings face expense-revenue squeeze; costs rising faster than controlled rents
Insurance, taxes, labor, fuel increases outpace rent growth; 2019 Tenant Protection Act limits recovery
Article XI property-tax PILOT program discussed as distressed building relief (up to 40-year benefit)
stories.summary: New York City's rent-stabilized housing stock is experiencing a structural economics crisis: operating expenses (insurance, real estate taxes, labor, repairs) are rising much faster than rents, which are constrained by rent-freeze policies and the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act. Owners have lost cost-recovery mechanisms, creating a scissors effect where expenses and revenues diverge. Article XI, a long-term property-tax abatement program (PILOT), is emerging as a potential lifeline for distressed stabilized buildings, offering dramatic tax relief for up to 40 years.
stories.impact: This is a major supply-side risk for NYC multifamily and market—distressed rent-stabilized buildings reduce overall housing stock viability and discourage reinvestment. For market-rate developers, persistent stabilized-building distress will put pressure on the city to either relax rent controls (unlikely) or accelerate conversions/decontrol (limited). More importantly, if Article XI becomes widespread, reduced tax revenue will shift burden to non-stabilized, market-rate properties via higher tax assessments, raising operating costs and reducing development ROI in Manhattan, outer boroughs. Developers should model elevated NYC property-tax scenarios and consider de-risking projects with long-term lease-up timelines.

stories.title: 107-Unit Charleston BTR Community Trades for $32M
stories.excerpt: Blaze Capital Partners offloaded the Charleston Row Townhomes, a 107-unit townhome property in Pineville, North Carolina. Blaze Capital Partners and Argosy Real Estate Partners acquired the asset in July 2022 for $32 million. The property was 98% occupied at the time of sale. Berkadia’s Caleb Troop, Thomas Colaiezzi and Matt Robertson and Drew Kwiatkowski of Berkadia Charlotte led the sale on Blaze Capital. The buyer was not disclosed. Located at 11945 Crooked Stick Place and built in 1969, the community offers two- and three-bedroom townhome units, with sizes ranging from 1,162 to over 1,700 square feet. Rents range from$1,725-$2,675. The townhome residences feature private patios and private one- or two-car garages. Charleston Row Townhomes is strategically located in Pineville within Charlotte’s highly sought-after South Charlotte corridor, placing residents in the heart of an employment-rich and amenity-driven submarket. stories.summary: Blaze Capital Partners and Argosy Real Estate Partners exited the Charleston Row Townhomes, a 107-unit townhome community in Pineville, North Carolina, at $32M—the same price paid in July 2022. The property was 98% occupied at time of sale and features two and three-bedroom units (1,162–1,700 SF) with private patios and garages, renting between $1,725 and $2,675. The property is positioned in Charlotte's sought-after South Charlotte submarket.
stories.impact: Flat pricing over 3.5 years on a stabilized, occupied asset signals a reset in Charlotte's market expectations post-rate shock. Lack of price appreciation despite high occupancy and location in a premier submarket suggests cap rates are still compressing or buyer demand is selective. For South Charlotte developers, this signals a buyer's pause on transitional/stabilized assets; new-build development with differentiated product and modern amenities likely commands better pricing power. Monitor South Charlotte land availability and entitlement velocity—repriced acquisitions may temporarily slow new supply, supporting near-term rent growth.

stories.title: Every Industry Eventually Learns a Shared Language. Data Centers Are Next.
stories.excerpt: One question has stayed with me since my last column on data center disclosure: How do standards emerge in an industry where every project is different? It is an important question because nothing about today’s data center market looks standardized. Every project is different. Every community asks different questions. Every developer tells a slightly different story. Yet history suggests that industries almost never begin with standards. They grow into them. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU The reason is straightforward. As industries mature, inconsistent information becomes expensive. Investors, lenders, insurers, regulators and customers all reach the same conclusion. Comparing projects is easier when everyone speaks the same language. The pattern repeats itself across industries. Finance eventually adopted Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) because investors needed confidence that financial statements meant the same thing from one company to the next. The standards did not make companies identical. They made companies comparable. Real estate followed a similar path. Residential appraisers do not prepare a different report for every lender. Standardized appraisal forms such as the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report, also known as Form 1004, became common because investors buying mortgages needed comparable information. The form did not standardize houses. It standardized how houses were described. Green building tells the same story. LEED began as a voluntary certification developed by the U.S. Green Building Council. Developers pursued certification because tenants, investors and lenders increasingly viewed it as a credible signal of quality and performance. Only later did many municipalities incorporate LEED into procurement requirements, incentives and public policy. bullets: Industry lacks standardized data center metrics; every project disclosure differs
Finance adopted GAAP, real estate adopted uniform appraisal forms—standardization drives comparability
Data center market approaching maturity; lenders, investors, insurers demanding consistent language
stories.summary: Data center markets lack standardized disclosure and underwriting frameworks—unlike mature industries (finance via GAAP, real estate via uniform appraisal forms), every data center project tells a different story, complicating investor comparisons and regulatory assessment. The author argues history shows that as industries mature, inconsistent information becomes expensive and standards emerge organically. Investors, lenders, insurers, and regulators will eventually demand consistent metrics and definitions across data center projects.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact on multifamily, but signals that data center standardization is coming, which could accelerate institutional capital flows into the sector once benchmarking clarity emerges. Indirectly, if data center markets crystallize faster than anticipated, they may attract hyperscale capital and labor to new markets (e.g., AI hubs), creating secondary-market demographic and job tailwinds for residential developers in data center gateway metros. Conversely, data center development consumes industrial land and labor; competition for construction crews and materials in data center-heavy markets (Austin, Phoenix, Virginia) may elevate multifamily construction costs and timelines.

stories.title: Princeton Developer Obtains Financing for Phase III of 374-Unit Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Aconcagua Group obtained a $35 million construction loan for the third and final phase of development for Casa Princeton, a multifamily residential community located at 12867 SW 248th Street in Princeton, Florida. S3 Capital provided the loan. Berkadia arranged the financing with a team led by Charles Foschini and Christopher Apone. T&G Constructors, the general contractor for Phases I and II, will continue in the same role for Phase III. Casa Princeton Phase III will comprise a 162-unit eight-story building and a two-story structured parking garage, bringing the overall community to a total of 374-units. The development will offer one- and two-bedroom apartments and expand the community’s shared amenity package, which includes a clubhouse and event space, co-working areas, a swimming pool, fitness center, playground, dog park and landscaped outdoor areas. The first two phases of Casa Princeton total 212 units. Phase I has been delivered and stabilized, and Phase II was delivered in March 2026 and is currently approximately 40% leased. stories.summary: Aconcagua Group obtained a $35M construction loan from S3 Capital for Phase III of Casa Princeton, a 374-unit multifamily community in Princeton, Florida (southwest of Miami). Phase III will add a 162-unit, eight-story building with structured parking to the existing community. Phase I is stabilized; Phase II was delivered in March 2026 and is currently about 40% leased, indicating healthy absorption in South Florida's market.
stories.impact: South Florida continues to attract speculative multifamily capital and construction financing—Phase II's 40% lease-up ~3 months post-delivery is solid for a new-build in a high-supply submarket, suggesting underlying demand. Completed Phase I stabilization signals rent-growth and lease velocity are supporting refinance and phase advancement. For developers, Casa Princeton's financing approval and Phase II absorption validate continued South Florida multifamily viability despite recent overbuilding; however, monitor Phase II and Phase III lease-up rates closely—if Phase III plateaus below 60% at 9 months, it signals over-saturation in Miami-Dade's rental market and would dampen future groundbreakings.

stories.title: Portman to Add 714K-SF Houston Warehouse Project to Growing Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Portman closed on the land and construction loan for Gateway 1960, a three-building, Class-A industrial park encompassing 714,233 square feet in Houston. The closings pave the way for development, which will begin this month. Portman will deliver Gateway 1960 in Q3 2027. Gateway 1960 includes a 440,323-square-foot cross-dock building, a 157,723-square-foot front-load building and a 116,293-square-foot rear-load building. Partners is leading marketing and leasing for Gateway 1960 on behalf of Portman. Gateway 1960's Q3 2027 timeline means supply will hit the Houston industrial market in peak e-commerce season. Indirectly, healthy industrial construction financing supports labor demand in Houston and signals continued logistics-sector confidence; this job growth (drivers, warehouse staff, local management) will support rental demand in Houston's outer-ring suburban markets (Katy, Pearland, Fort Bend County). Developers should track industrial occupancy rates and lease rates in Houston as a leading indicator of broader metro job market health.

stories.title: New York City’s Next Multifamily Shortage? Buildings to Buy.
stories.excerpt: For years, nearly every conversation about New York City multifamily has centered around one shortage: housing. We don’t have enough apartments. We don’t build fast enough. Vacancy remains tight, construction is expensive, and the regulatory environment makes adding new supply increasingly difficult. But there is another shortage developing that investors and owners should be paying close attention to: a shortage of multifamily buildings to buy. I am talking about quality buildings worth buying — free-market apartment buildings with minimal regulatory risk hurdles. Lev Mavashev. PHOTO: Courtesy Alpha Realty That may sound strange after several years when buyers had the upper hand and plenty of owners struggled to get their pricing. But the market is changing. Capital is coming back faster than quality inventory is coming to market, and the numbers are starting to reflect that. According to Alpha Realty’s second-quarter 2026 multifamily market report, New York City recorded 304 multifamily transactions during the three months ended June 30, up 10.5 percent from the first quarter and 2.4 percent year-over-year. That followed 275 transactions in the first quarter, which itself was up nearly 20 percent from the prior year. In other words, despite elevated borrowing costs, transaction velocity continues to improve. Most of the multifamily transactions have been for free-market and newer construction buildings. What’s interesting is that multifamily buildings with 20-plus units accounted for 112 transactions in the second quarter, up 24.4 percent from the quarter before and 8.7 percent from a year earlier. Those assets represented $872.2 million, or roughly 57 percent of all New York City multifamily dollar volume during the quarter. That follows an already strong first quarter, when properties with at least 20 units accounted for $1.06 billion, or approximately 61 percent of citywide multifamily volume. bullets: NYC multifamily bottleneck shifting from housing shortage to shortage of quality buildings to buy
Alpha Realty reports 304 transactions Q2 2026 (up 10.5% QoQ, +2.4% YoY); capital returning faster than inventory
Free-market apartment buildings with low regulatory risk in tight supply; buyer demand exceeding product
stories.summary: New York City's multifamily market is experiencing a reversal: instead of a housing shortage, the constraint is now a shortage of quality, free-market apartment buildings worth acquiring. According to Alpha Realty's Q2 2026 report, NYC recorded 304 multifamily transactions (+10.5% QoQ, +2.4% YoY), signaling capital is returning faster than stabilized, low-regulatory-risk inventory is coming to market. The imbalance is pushing acquisition prices upward.
stories.impact: This is a critical supply-side signal for NYC multifamily developers: cap rates are compressing and buyer competition is intensifying for stabilized core assets, likely pushing sellers to expect higher valuations. For developers, this creates a two-tier market: (1) core stabilized assets face buyer competition and limited availability, limiting value-add opportunities, and (2) development-stage projects (new construction, conversions) face higher acquisition costs for land/buildings, raising hurdle rates. Developers should prioritize large-block land assemblies in lower-density outer-borough submarkets (Staten Island, outer Queens, Bronx) where land is cheaper and regulatory risk lower, or target opportunistic conversions (office-to-residential) where acquisition basis may be lower. Expect continued NYC multifamily pricing pressure unless new construction supply accelerates or regulatory risk is relaxed.

stories.title: AI-Searched Public Records Alone Insufficient for Title Decision-Making: Study
stories.excerpt: Artificial intelligence-only searches of public records aren’t enough to provide reliable title decision-making at scale, according to a new study by DataTrace, a national provider of property and ownership data and title automation solutions. The company’s analysis, “AI Title Search Tested in the Real World: What Accuracy, Risk and Readiness Really Look Like,” compares AI-only with title plant-supported searches to evaluate completeness, accuracy and insurability. (A title plant is an index of all of the recorded events that affect a property, unique in that it’s posted, or indexed, as the official legal description of the property.) “The study is a projection of potential risk, and the opportunity to look at specific — what we would call, gaps — where the AI solution alone was used,” said Annette Cotton, senior vice president and chief data officer at DataTrace. “It predicts if that property had been insured upon, for instance, what could have been an outcome in terms of not being able to report on, address, or remediate that gap. “Our analysis demonstrates that AI performs best when it operates on a foundation of structured, validated title data, rather than fragmented county-level public records. The speed of AI creates value, but only when paired with the confidence, completeness and accuracy needed for insurable title decisioning. The future isn’t AI versus title professionals. It’s AI powered by trusted title data and guided by experienced title experts. That’s how the industry scales automation without sacrificing confidence or insurability.” DataTrace manages more than 2,000 title plants nationally. The new study is a follow-up to DataTrace’s first white paper on its position concerning title plant value, said Cotton. “This was intended to try to answer more details about that and what the impact would have been based on those early findings when we were doing the AI testing against traditional examination.” Among the current study’s
bullets: DataTrace study finds AI-only public record searches insufficient for reliable title decisions at scale
AI gaps appear on structured, indexed data; title plant (official property record index) remains necessary
Incomplete AI-only searches create insurability risk and potential remediation gaps
stories.summary: A DataTrace study comparing AI-only versus title plant-supported title searches found that artificial intelligence alone is insufficient for reliable, scalable title decision-making. AI performs best on structured, indexed data but misses gaps that could create insurability and remediation risks. Title plants—official indices of recorded events affecting a property—remain a necessary foundation for comprehensive title underwriting.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development, but signals that transaction automation will remain incomplete without hybrid AI + human/data infrastructure. For developers, this reinforces that due diligence timelines cannot be aggressively compressed without title-plant backed underwriting, especially for complex land assemblies or distressed acquisitions. On financing side, lenders will likely continue requiring full title policies rather than relying on AI abstracts alone, potentially extending closing timelines. This is an indirect friction cost for deal velocity but does not materially change development underwriting or market risk.
